title: Camera Offline and Health Monitor
dataSources: NVR object-detection (`frigate:event`), camera health (`camera:health`), alarm arm/disarm and life-safety (`alarm:event`), lock access (`lock:access`), plate recognition (`plate:detection`), doorbell (`doorbell:event`).
app: Frigate / Blue Iris NVR object-detection events, camera health, alarm and smart-lock logs, and licence-plate recognition via MQTT and Splunk HEC.
spl:
index=personal sourcetype=camera:health
| stats latest(_time) as last_seen, latest(status) as status by camera
| eval mins_silent=round((now()-last_seen)/60,0), offline=if(mins_silent>10,1,0)
| where offline=1
description: Alerts when a security camera stops reporting, because a camera that is quietly offline is worse than no camera at all.
value: Cameras fail silently and you only notice when you need the footage; a heartbeat check catches an outage the day it happens.
implementation: Ingest camera heartbeats or status; alert when a camera has not reported for several minutes.
visualization: Table of cameras with minutes since last seen and offline flag.
detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites

• **Splunk**: Splunk Enterprise ≥9.0 or Splunk Cloud — a single-instance home lab is fine. Create `index=personal` with 90–365 day retention (`indexes.conf`).
• **HEC token**: Settings → Data Inputs → HTTP Event Collector → New Token → index `personal`. Store the token in your connector's environment (never commit it to git).
• **Upstream product**: Personal HEC index — HTTP Event Collector token on index=personal.
• **Subcategory context**: Home Security & Surveillance — typical feeds: NVR object-detection (`frigate:event`), camera health (`camera:health`), alarm arm/disarm and life-safety (`alarm:event`), lock access (`lock:access`), plate recognition (`plate:detection`), doorbell .
• **Sourcetypes in this search**: `camera:health`.
• **Network**: The connector host must reach both the vendor API/MQTT broker and your Splunk HEC port (8088/tcp).

## Step 1 — Configure data collection

Route **Personal HEC index** events into `index=personal` with `sourcetype=camera:health`.

**Collection method:** HTTP Event Collector token on index=personal.

**Reference endpoint / path:** `POST https://<splunk>:8088/services/collector/event`.

**Suggested poll interval:** depends on upstream connector.

**Key fields to extract:** `sourcetype-specific — see search filters`.

**Typical connector stack:** Frigate / Blue Iris NVR object-detection events, camera health, alarm and smart-lock logs, and licence-plate recognition via MQTT and Splunk HEC..

**Author notes:** Ingest camera heartbeats or status; alert when a camera has not reported for several minutes.


Example HEC payload shape:

```json
{"index": "personal", "sourcetype": "camera:health", "event": { ... vendor fields ... }}
```

Verify ingestion with:

```spl
index=personal sourcetype=camera:health earliest=-24h | head 20
```

## Step 2 — Create the search and alert

This search implements **Camera Offline and Health Monitor** over `personal` data (primarily `sourcetype=camera:health`) across the full search range. It applies numeric thresholds on `mins_silent` (> 10) after latest — tune these constants to your household baseline.

**Fields this search depends on:** `camera`, `mins_silent`. Confirm each is populated before scheduling alerts.

```spl
index=personal sourcetype=camera:health
| stats latest(_time) as last_seen, latest(status) as status by camera
| eval mins_silent=round((now()-last_seen)/60,0), offline=if(mins_silent>10,1,0)
| where offline=1
```

## Step 3 — Validate

**(a) Compare to vendor UI:** Splunk Search → index=personal | stats count by sourcetype. Totals for the same day/week should match within connector lag (usually one poll interval).

**(b) Field presence:**

```spl
index=personal sourcetype=camera:health earliest=-7d
| head 50
| table camera, mins_silent
```

Every column the detection uses should be non-null on recent rows.

**(c) Volume sanity:**

```spl
index=personal sourcetype=camera:health earliest=-30d
| timechart span=1d count
```

Flatlines usually mean a broken token, expired OAuth refresh, or HEC URL change.

**(d) Threshold calibration:** Profile `mins_silent` before alerting:

```spl
index=personal sourcetype=camera:health earliest=-30d
| stats perc50(mins_silent) AS p50 perc90(mins_silent) AS p90 perc99(mins_silent) AS p99 max(mins_silent) AS hi
```

## Step 4 — Operationalize

Create a companion dashboard titled `UC-25.18.4: Personal evidence` with the following panel layout:

**Panel 1 — Table Of Cameras With Minutes Since Last Seen And Offline Flag (the key fields):** Configure according to standard Splunk visualization patterns for this panel type.


Time picker defaults: set to last 30 days with named presets for 24h, 7d, 30d, 90d, and 1y — the auditor needs all five windows without retyping. Enable scheduled PDF export for the full dashboard on the regulation's reporting cadence.

## Step 5 — Troubleshooting

**Personal HEC index — no Personal HEC index events / missing fields:** If `camera:health` stops updating, re-check HEC token, index `personal`, and firewall to port 8088. Search `index=_internal sourcetype=splunkd group=http_event_collector` for rejection reasons. Confirm the Personal HEC index connector script is still running (`systemctl status` or cron log).

**Personal HEC index — NULL values in extracted fields:** The Personal HEC index JSON export shape drifted — compare a raw event (`index=personal sourcetype=camera:health | head 1 | spath`) against the field names in Step 2. Re-map in the connector before changing the SPL.

**Personal HEC index — API error / auth denied (401/403):** Refresh tokens expire on most consumer APIs — re-authorize the scripted input, update `passwords.conf` / env vars, and verify the vendor developer app is not in sandbox mode.

**Personal HEC index — endpoint timeout / HTTP 429 throttling:** Back off the poll interval in the connector; Personal HEC index APIs often cap requests per 15 minutes on free tiers.

**Stale dashboard:** Confirm the saved search `dispatch.earliest_time` covers enough history for your `aggregation` buckets.
